partial_case.facts: The resident lives in a flat on the fifth floor of a block with her children, one of whom is very young. The resident and 2 of her children are vulnerable and have health conditions. When she moved into the property it was a new build within a defects period. She complained to the landlord about various repairs, the suitability of the property, and its handling of other matters. She also made a later complaint about its handling of electrical repairs in her kitchen. On or around 20 October 2024 the resident made a stage 1 complaint about: repairs to her balcony door had taken 3 years to complete after she first reported the safety hazard for her children; her windows could be opened by her children and were not safe; ASB in the communal areas caused by youths and parcels having been stolen; not having received an apology or compensation for the time the lift was broken; the landlord's slow response when a neighbour died and the impact this had on her mental health; having £23,000 worth of arrears added to her rent account when she was in receipt of benefits to pay her rent; having raised complaints previously but the landlord not responding. On 27 December 2024 the landlord attended a repair for a fault with the electrics in the resident's kitchen. It said it needed a follow-on appointment. On 19 February 2025 the resident made a stage 1 complaint about the landlord's delay in repairing the electrics in her kitchen.
partial_case.ground_truth_outcome: Severe maladministration for repairs handling; maladministration for ASB, rent arrears, and complaint handling; no maladministration for death of neighbour; property suitability complaint outside jurisdiction

key_reasoning_quotes.text: There was severe maladministration as the landlord unreasonably delayed in repairing the balcony doors. It failed and continues to fail to repair the windows to make them safe.

The landlord had knowledge of the potential safety hazard under the Housing Health and Safety Rating System (HHSRS). Falling between levels, including from a balcony, is a hazard under the HHSRS. Landlords have an obligation to remove or reduce hazards.
In the absence of any evidence that the landlord has followed its ASB policy, and with the problem ongoing, there was maladministration.
The landlord has failed to demonstrate that it acknowledged this, communicated with her or reassured her that she would not lose her home.

partial_case.facts: The resident lives in a fifth-floor flat with her children; the resident and two children are vulnerable and have health conditions, and the property was a new build within a defects period when she moved in. The complaint concerned repairs to balcony doors, windows, lift and kitchen electrics; reports of ASB and thefts; the death of a neighbour; rent arrears; suitability of the property; and complaint handling. On or around 20 October 2024, the resident made a stage 1 complaint about balcony-door repairs taking three years, unsafe windows, ASB and parcel thefts, lack of apology or compensation for the lift, the landlord’s response after a neighbour died, £23,000 arrears being added to her rent account, and previous complaints not being answered. On 27 December 2024, the landlord attended a repair for a fault with the kitchen electrics and said a follow-on appointment was needed. On 3 January 2025, the landlord provided its stage 2 response to the first complaint, apologised for delays in repairing balcony doors, said it would arrange window restrictors, accepted an ASB issue on the estate, said Housing Benefit had been deducted due to a system error in April 2024 and believed this had been resolved by September 2024, and did not uphold the complaint. On 19 February 2025, the resident made a second stage 1 complaint about delay repairing the kitchen electrics; the landlord repaired the electrical fault on 24 February 2025. On 25 February 2025, the landlord provided its stage 1 response to the second complaint, apologised for delay and said it partially upheld the complaint; the resident escalated the same day and asked for reimbursement and/or compensation. On 4 April 2025, the landlord provided its stage 2 response to the second complaint, upheld it, apologised for communication failings, and offered a £100 goodwill gesture. The resident referred the complaint to the Ombudsman because she was dissatisfied with the final responses and said she had not been compensated for inconvenience and distress caused by repairs and delays.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: There were multiple and significant failings in the landlord’s handling of repairs. It delayed unreasonably to complete repairs to the balcony doors and delayed in repairing the kitchen electrics. It has failed to resolve the windows hazard.
Cumulatively there was severe maladministration, which caused substantial distress, worry, inconvenience, time and trouble for the resident over a number of years.
The landlord was ultimately responsible for repairs to external doors under the tenancy agreement. It failed to complete repairs within its policy timeframe or any notion of a reasonable time.
Falling between levels, including from a balcony, is a hazard under the HHSRS. Landlords have an obligation to remove or reduce hazards.
In the absence of any evidence that the landlord has followed its ASB policy, and with the problem ongoing, there was maladministration.
The landlord has failed to demonstrate that it acknowledged this, communicated with her or reassured her that she would not lose her home.
Overall, there was maladministration. The landlord did not follow its complaints policy, did not retain or provide evidence and could not show it acknowledged either complaint or escalation request.
